In [[mathematics]], the '''integral of a correspondence''' is a generalization of the [[Integral | integration]] of [[Function (mathematics)|single-valued functions]] to [[ Set-valued function|correspondences]] (i.e., set-valued functions). 

The first notion of the integral of a correspondence is due to [[Robert Aumann| Aumann]] in 1965,<ref name = "aumann1965">{{cite journal |last1=Aumann |first1=Robert J. |author1-link=Robert Aumann |title=Integrals of Set-Valued Functions* |journal=Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications |date=1965 |volume=12 |pages=1–12 |doi=10.1016/0022-247X(65)90049-1}}</ref> with a different == Preliminaries ==

=== Correspondences ===

A ''correspondence'' <math> \varphi: X  \rightrightarrows Y</math> is a function <math>\varphi : X \rightarrow \mathcal{P} (Y)</math>, where <math>\mathcal{P} (Y)</math> is the [[power set]] of <math>Y</math>. That is, <math>\varphi</math> assigns each point <math>x \in X</math> with a set <math>\varphi(x) \subset Y</math>.

=== Selections ===

A [[Choice_function#Choice_function_of_a_multivalued_map|''selection'']] <math>f</math> of a correspondence <math>\varphi: X  \rightrightarrows Y</math> is a function <math>f: X \rightarrow Y</math> such that <math>f(x) \in \varphi(x)</math> for every <math>x \in X</math>. 

If <math>X</math> can be seen as a [[measure space]] <math>(X, \mathcal X, \mu)</math> and <math>Y</math> as a [[Banach space]] <math>(Y, || \cdot ||)</math>, then one can define a ''measurable selection'' <math>f</math> as an  <math>\mathcal X</math>-[[measurable function]]{{r|g=nb|r= Measurable in the sense of [[Bochner measurable]]: there exists a sequence <math>(\psi_n)_n</math> of simple functions from <math>X</math> to <math>Y</math> such that <math>\lim_{n \to \infty} ||f(x) - \psi_n(x)|| = 0</math> for μ-almost all <math>x \in X</math>.}} <math>f</math> such that <math>f(x) \in \varphi(x)</math> for [[Almost everywhere | μ-almost all]] <math>x \in X</math>.<ref name = "molchanov2017"/>{{r|g=nb|r= A stronger definition sometimes used requires <math>f</math> to be measurable and <math>f(x) \in \varphi(x)</math> for all <math>x \in X</math>. <ref name = "border1991"/>}}

== Definitions == 

=== The Aumann integral===

Let <math>(X, \mathcal X, \mu)</math> be a measure space and <math>(Y, ||\cdot ||)</math> a Banach space. If <math>\varphi : X\rightrightarrows Y </math> is a correspondence, then the ''Aumann integral'' of <math>\varphi</math> is defined as 

:<math>\int_X \varphi d \mu := \left\{\int_X f d \mu : f \text{ is a measurable selection of } \varphi\right\}</math>

where the integrals <math>\int_X f d \mu </math> are [[Bochner integral]]s.

'''Example''': let the underlying measure space be <math>([0,1], \mathcal L, \lambda)</math>, and a correspondence <math>\varphi: [0,1] \rightrightarrows \mathbb R</math> be defined as <math>\varphi(x) = \{2, 3\}</math> for all <math>x \in [0,1]</math>. Then the Aumman integral of <math>\varphi</math> is <math>\int_X \varphi d \lambda = [2, 3]</math>.

=== The Debreu integral===

Debreu's approach to the integration of a correspondence is more restrictive and cumbersome, but directly yields extensions of usual theorems from the integration theory of functions to the integration of correspondences, such as [[Lebesgue]]'s [[Dominated convergence theorem]].<ref name = "klein-thompson1984"/> It uses [[Rådström's embedding theorem]] to identify convex and compact valued correspondences with subsets of a real Banach space, over which [[Bochner integral | Bochner integration]] is straightforward.<ref name = "debreu1967"/>

Let <math>(X, \mathcal X, \mu)</math> be a measure space, <math>(Y, ||\cdot ||)</math> a Banach space, and <math>\mathcal K \subset \mathcal P(Y)</math> the set of all its convex and compact subsets. Let <math>\varphi: X \to \mathcal K</math> be a convex and compact valued correspondence from <math>X</math> to <math>Y</math>. By [[Rådström's embedding theorem]], <math>\mathcal K</math> can be [[Embedding#Metric_spaces| isometrically embedded]] as a [[convex cone]] <math>C</math> in a real Banach space <math>(\mathcal Y, || \cdot ||_{\mathcal Y})</math>, in such a way that addition and multiplication by nonnegative real numbers in <math>\mathcal Y</math> induces the corresponding operation in <math>\mathcal K</math>. 

Let <math>\varphi^*: X  \rightrightarrows C</math> be the "image" of <math>\varphi</math> under the embedding defined above, in the sense that <math>\varphi^*(x) \subset C</math> is the image of <math>\varphi(x)</math> under this embedding for every <math>x \in X</math>. For each pair of <math>\mathcal X</math>-simple functions <math>f, g : X \to C</math>, define the metric <math>\Delta(f, g) = \int_X ||f - g||_{\mathcal Y} d \mu</math>. 

Then we say that <math>\varphi</math> is integrable if <math>\varphi^*</math> is integrable in the following sense: there exists a sequence of <math>\mathcal X</math>-simple functions <math>(f_n)_n</math> from <math>X</math> to <math>C</math> which are [[Cauchy_sequence#In_a_metric_space| Cauchy]] in the metric <math>\Delta</math> and [[Convergence in measure |converge in measure]] to <math>\varphi^*</math>. In this case, we define the integral of <math>\varphi^*</math> to be

:<math>\int_X \varphi^* d \mu := \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_X f_n d \mu \in C</math>

where the integrals <math>\int_X f_n d \mu</math> are again simply [[Bochner integral]]s in the space <math>(\mathcal Y, || \cdot ||_{\mathcal Y})</math>, and the result still belongs <math>C</math> since it is a convex cone. We then uniquely identify the ''Debreu integral of <math>\varphi</math>'' as<ref name = "molchanov2017"/>

:<math>\int_X \varphi d \mu := E  \in \mathcal K </math>

such that <math>E^* = \int_X \varphi^* d \mu \in C</math>. Since every embedding is injective and surjective onto its image, the Debreu integral is unique and well-defined.
